systems.name: Solo Fingerstyle Arrangement System
systems.summary: Carter's central system for reducing a full-band jazz standard to a solo fingerstyle guitar arrangement. The system operates over four voice/texture categories (melody, harmonization interval, bass, accompaniment texture) and governs how a player moves between them and alters each layer. The workflow proceeds from tune selection through melodic placement, harmonization with thirds/sixths/tenths, bass anchoring, and density calibration. The ear is the final arbiter throughout.

members.name: Melody Voice
members.summary: The top voice; a single-note melody from a lead sheet, stems up, typically in a guitar-friendly key above the fourth string D threshold.

members.name: Thirds Harmonization
members.summary: A harmony note a diatonic third below the melody, adjusted major or minor against the chord symbol.

members.name: Sixths Harmonization
members.summary: A harmony note a diatonic sixth below the melody. Key note must sit on top; sixth below.

members.name: Tenths Harmonization
members.summary: An octave-plus-third below the melody. Functions as an independent bass voice with its own rhythm.

members.name: Root / Root-Fifth Bass
members.summary: A foundational bass layer using the chord root alone or alternating root and perfect fifth.

members.name: Walking Bass
members.summary: A quarter-note bass line using scale-step passing tones and chromatic approach notes between chord roots.

members.name: Arpeggio / Broken-Chord Accompaniment
members.summary: Arpeggio patterns assigning p to lower strings and i-m-a to upper strings with free stroke.

members.name: Comping Texture
members.summary: Sparse, responsive chordal punctuation calibrated to the melody's activity level.

traversal_rules.name: Melody Range Gate before harmonizing
traversal_rules.summary: Before selecting a harmonization member, verify the melody sits above the fourth-string D threshold; if not, raise it an octave.

references.quote_excerpt: tunes with a preponderance of notes lower than D, fourth string, are too low for two-part arranging

traversal_rules.name: Density Inversion: busy melody implies sparse bass
traversal_rules.summary: When transitioning between melody and bass texture, invert rhythmic density.

references.quote_excerpt: If the rhythm of the melody is busy and many-noted, you can complement it by playing longer notes in the bass

traversal_rules.name: Walking bass during melodic rests; comping during sustained melody
traversal_rules.summary: Switch to walking bass when the melody is inactive; shift to comping texture when melody notes are sustained.

references.quote_excerpt: Sometimes a walking bass style is used and sometimes a measure has a riff while the melody is not active

traversal_rules.name: Arpeggio must not exceed melody ceiling
traversal_rules.summary: When using arpeggio accompaniment, never allow the arpeggio sweep to reach higher than the melody voice.

references.quote_excerpt: watch that your choice of arpeggiation does not reach higher than the melody

traversal_rules.name: Tenths move on independent rhythm, not parallel to melody
traversal_rules.summary: When traversing from melody to tenths, give the tenth its own rhythmic value.

references.quote_excerpt: You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement

modification_rules.name: Thirds major/minor adjustment against chord symbol
modification_rules.summary: When applying a third below the melody, consult the chord symbol and the TABLE OF THIRDS.

references.quote_excerpt: Try putting thirds below each melody note. Follow the chord symbols to check for the correct third

modification_rules.name: Sixths: key note must be on top
modification_rules.summary: When applying sixth harmonization, the key note must remain on top with the harmony a sixth below.

references.quote_excerpt: By convention, scales harmonized in sixths have the key note of each scale on top

modification_rules.name: Sixths major/minor adjustment same as thirds
modification_rules.summary: Apply the same major/minor adjustment discipline to sixths as to thirds.

references.quote_excerpt: take a familiar tune and harmonize it with diatonic sixths

modification_rules.name: Thirds harmonization requires bass anchor for three-voice texture
modification_rules.summary: A section harmonized only in thirds needs a root or root/fifth bass added.

references.quote_excerpt: A melody harmonized only in thirds can progress by itself for a section of a tune, but probably not for the entire song

modification_rules.name: Add major/minor third in bass when melody is harmonically ambiguous
modification_rules.summary: When the melody note belongs equally to major and minor, the accompaniment must supply the third.

references.quote_excerpt: The accompaniment needs the major or minor third to clarify the specific harmony

modification_rules.name: Compositional restraint: deploy arranging devices sparingly
modification_rules.summary: A complete arrangement should use arranging devices economically.

references.quote_excerpt: here is a tune that is not cluttered with every arranging device, but is still totally whole

modification_rules.name: Altered fifth: raise or lower fifth per chord symbol
modification_rules.summary: When the chord symbol carries #5 or b5, raise or lower the fifth by a half step.

references.quote_excerpt: If the chord is C7#5, raise the fifth a half step

modification_rules.name: Abandon arpeggio when melody leaps wildly
modification_rules.summary: If the melody continually leaps in large intervals, arpeggio accompaniment is not appropriate.

references.quote_excerpt: If you notice that the melody continually leaps up and down wildly, abandon arpeggiation

systems.name: Cycle-of-Fifths Voice Leading System
systems.summary: Carter's professional-level system for generating smooth harmonic progressions through the cycle of fifths, treating harmony as several independent moving voices rather than static chord shapes.

members.name: Major Seventh Chord (I, IV)
members.summary: Two occur per major key. Voiced as open-position fragments.

members.name: Dominant Seventh Chord (V7)
members.summary: One per major key. Contains the tritone that pulls by half steps to the I chord.

members.name: Minor Seventh Chord (II, III, VI)
members.summary: Three per major key. In II-V-I: voiced as root + seventh.

members.name: Half-Diminished Seventh Chord (VII)
members.summary: One per major key; functions as a passing or substitution chord.

members.name: Diminished Seventh Chord
members.summary: The hamburger helper passing chord connecting adjacent diatonic chords.

members.name: Fourths / Tritones Rootless Voicing
members.summary: Voicing pairs alternating fourths and tritones, omitting root and fifth.

traversal_rules.name: Move down a fifth or up a fourth through the cycle
traversal_rules.summary: On guitar, substitute up a fourth for down a fifth to stay in position.

references.quote_excerpt: When you run out of room, move up a fourth instead of down a fifth

traversal_rules.name: V7 tritone resolves by half step to I
traversal_rules.summary: The tritone interval of V7 resolves inward by half step to root and third of I.

references.quote_excerpt: the unresolved Bb and E being pulled by the A and F in the resolved F chord

traversal_rules.name: Conceive harmony as moving voices, not chord shapes
traversal_rules.summary: Track the linear motion of individual voices rather than placing static chord shapes.

references.quote_excerpt: If you think of harmonic movement as several moving voices rather than a glob of dots

traversal_rules.name: Diminished seventh as chromatic connector
traversal_rules.summary: Insert a diminished seventh chord as a chromatic passing chord between diatonic chords.

references.quote_excerpt: In many cases the diminished seventh chord is the in-between, the hamburger helper

traversal_rules.name: II-V-I as the foundational traversal unit
traversal_rules.summary: Move through chords primarily as II-V-I units.

references.quote_excerpt: The most common harmonic movement in jazz is II-V-l

traversal_rules.name: Two-beat harmonic rhythm default for cycle practice
traversal_rules.summary: Change harmony every two beats; begin each group with the root.

references.quote_excerpt: the harmony changes every two beats

modification_rules.name: Redistribute chord tones across octaves for playability
modification_rules.summary: Convert close-position to open-position by moving the third up an octave.

references.quote_excerpt: the third of the chord has been moved an octave higher

modification_rules.name: Fourths/tritones voicing omits root and fifth
modification_rules.summary: Omit root and fifth; delegate root coverage to the bassist.

references.quote_excerpt: There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord

modification_rules.name: Tritone substitution: replace V7 with chord a tritone away
modification_rules.summary: A V7 may be replaced by a dominant seventh a tritone away.

references.quote_excerpt: chord substitution material focuses on tritone substitutions

modification_rules.name: Bidirectional practice: general to specific and vice versa
modification_rules.summary: Extract cycle passages for specific tunes; generalize tune passages through the cycle.

references.quote_excerpt: create specific examples from general exercises and to make general exercises from specific examples

systems.name: Jazz Performance Structure System
systems.summary: Carter's system governing the structural units of a jazz performance: intros, endings, turnarounds, tags, and modulations. All grounded in the I-V7 relationship and the cycle of fifths.

members.name: Introduction
members.summary: A two- or four-bar framework; must end on V7 to resolve into the tune.

members.name: Ending
members.summary: A closing structure using V7-I or IV-I; produced from any intro by omitting the final V7.

members.name: Vamp
members.summary: A repeating intro used with singers; repeated until the singer cues.

members.name: Turnaround
members.summary: Final two measures of each chorus; functions as a two-measure intro.

members.name: Tag / Coda
members.summary: Extension of the final chorus; replace final I with V7.

members.name: Modulation
members.summary: Key change via V7 borrow, back-cycling, or II-V7-I from target key.

traversal_rules.name: Intro must end on V7
traversal_rules.summary: Every intro must conclude on V7 to resolve into the tune.

references.quote_excerpt: The last chord of the intro must be a V7 or V7 substitute

traversal_rules.name: Omit final V7 to convert intro into ending
traversal_rules.summary: Any intro becomes an ending by omitting the final V7.

references.quote_excerpt: What if you just did not play the G13 on the third beat? Your intro would become an instant ending

traversal_rules.name: Turnaround functions as two-measure intro
traversal_rules.summary: Two-measure intro material works as a turnaround.

references.quote_excerpt: whatever you would use as a two-measure intro of a tune you could use as a turnaround

traversal_rules.name: Tag replaces final I with V7
traversal_rules.summary: Execute a tag by replacing the final I chord with V7.

references.quote_excerpt: the replacement of the usual final I chord with a V7 or other substitute chord is required

modification_rules.name: Fastest modulation: borrow V7 from target key
modification_rules.summary: Use the last two beats to play V7 of the upcoming key.

references.quote_excerpt: You can modulate as fast as two beats. Use the last two beats to borrow V7

modification_rules.name: Back-cycling modulation from target V7
modification_rules.summary: Work backwards through the cycle of fifths from the target key V7.

references.quote_excerpt: Using the cycle of fifths as a method of movement, work backwards

modification_rules.name: II-V7-I modulation from target key
modification_rules.summary: Place the II chord of the upcoming key before V7 for smooth modulation.

references.quote_excerpt: the most common jazz progression unit is II-V7-I. Use it here then
